act.cpr: Start CPR (hard + fast, 30:2) and call the code
act.resume: Resume CPR right away for 2 min
act.hts: Hunt for reversible causes (Hs and Ts)
act.vagal: Vagal manoeuvre (blow into a syringe, legs up)

s.msg: A 55-year-old teacher grabs his chest and collapses. He's unresponsive and only gasping. You can't feel a carotid pulse.
s.ok: Unresponsive + not breathing normally (gasping counts as NOT breathing) + no pulse = cardiac arrest. Start compressions within 10 seconds and get help + a defibrillator. Every minute without CPR cuts survival by about 10%.

fb.sugar: Not now: no pulse means CPR first. Glucose can wait.
fb.epi: No IV yet and no compressions. CPR first.
fb.shock: No pads on and you don't know the rhythm yet. Start CPR while the defibrillator comes.

s.msg: Pads are on. CPR paused for a rhythm check. Look at the monitor.
s.ok: VF: chaotic, no QRS complexes. It's a SHOCKABLE rhythm, so defibrillate immediately (unsynchronised, everyone clear).

fb.epi: VF needs electricity first. Drugs come after the 2nd shock.
fb.sync: Synchronised shocks need a QRS to sync to. VF has none, so the machine would never fire. Use an unsynchronised shock.
fb.atro: Atropine is for slow rhythms with a pulse. This is VF.

s.msg: Shock delivered. What now?
s.ok: Straight back on the chest for 2 minutes. Even a successful shock leaves a stunned heart that barely pumps, so don't waste time on a pulse check.

fb.pulse: Checking a pulse right after a shock wastes precious seconds. CPR first, then check rhythm in 2 minutes.
fb.shock: Shocks are 2 minutes apart, with CPR in between.
fb.amio: Amiodarone is given after the 3rd shock. Right now: compressions.

s.msg: 2 minutes of CPR done. Rhythm check: still VF. You shock again and restart CPR. IV is in. Which drug now?
s.ok: After the 2nd shock: epinephrine, repeated every 3–5 minutes. It squeezes blood vessels (alpha effect) to push more blood to the heart and brain during compressions.

fb.amio: Amiodarone comes after the 3rd shock. Epinephrine first.
fb.atro: Atropine is not used in cardiac arrest any more.
fb.ade: Adenosine is for SVT with a pulse.

s.msg: Another 2 minutes. Rhythm check: STILL VF. You shock a 3rd time and resume CPR. Next drug?
s.ok: Refractory VF after the 3rd shock: amiodarone (or lidocaine). It blocks potassium channels and calms the irritable ventricle so the next shock is more likely to stick.

fb.epi: It's only been ~2 minutes since the last epinephrine. Next one in 3–5 min. Now: antiarrhythmic.
fb.calc: Calcium is for high potassium or calcium-channel-blocker poisoning, not routine VF.

s.msg: Rhythm check: the monitor now shows an organised rhythm.
s.ok: Organised rhythm on the monitor? Check for a pulse. It could be return of circulation (ROSC) or PEA (rhythm with no pulse).

fb.shock: Never shock an organised rhythm without checking. You could cause VF.
fb.epi: Check whether there's a pulse first.
fb.resume: With an organised rhythm, check the pulse first (under 10 seconds).

s.msg: Strong carotid pulse! BP 98/60. He's still unconscious.
s.ok: ROSC. Post-arrest care: secure the airway, aim for normal oxygen and CO₂, support blood pressure, 12-lead ECG (likely heart attack → cath lab to open the artery), and temperature control for brain protection.

fb.shock: He has a pulse. No shocks.
fb.epi: Bolus arrest-dose epinephrine with a pulse could cause dangerous hypertension and arrhythmias.
fb.wait: He needs active post-arrest care now: airway, BP, ECG, cath lab.

s.msg: A 60-year-old on the treadmill collapses. CPR is going, pads are on. Rhythm check: wide, fast, regular. No pulse.
s.ok: Pulseless VT is treated exactly like VF: unsynchronised shock, then CPR.

fb.sync: Synchronised cardioversion is for VT WITH a pulse. No pulse = defibrillate (unsynchronised).
fb.ade: Adenosine is for narrow-complex SVT with a pulse.
fb.amio: Shock first; amiodarone after the 3rd shock.

s.msg: Shocked. CPR resumed. 2 minutes later: still pulseless VT. You shock again. During CPR, which drug?
s.ok: Same as VF: epinephrine after the 2nd shock, every 3–5 minutes.

fb.calc: Only for specific causes like high potassium.

s.msg: Next rhythm check: organised rhythm and a pulse is back. BP 110/70.
s.ok: ROSC → post-arrest care. Find out why: ECG for a heart attack, electrolytes, and consider a defibrillator implant later if no reversible cause.

fb.resume: Pulse is back, so no compressions.
fb.shock: Never shock someone with a pulse and a normal rhythm.
fb.amio: Not needed routinely with a stable rhythm.

s.msg: Paramedics find an 80-year-old unresponsive, not breathing, no pulse. Pads on, monitor shows this. (Leads and gain checked: it's real.)
s.ok: Asystole: flatline, NOT shockable. Shocking a flatline does nothing. High-quality CPR is the treatment.

fb.shock: Shocking asystole doesn't help: there's no electrical chaos to reset. CPR.
fb.atro: Atropine was removed from the arrest algorithm years ago.
fb.pace: Pacing doesn't work in asystole arrest.

s.msg: CPR is going, IV in. What drug, and when?
s.ok: Non-shockable rhythm: give epinephrine AS SOON AS POSSIBLE, then every 3–5 minutes.

fb.amio: Amiodarone is only for shockable rhythms (VF/VT).
fb.calc: Only if there's a reason (high potassium, etc.).

s.msg: Still asystole after 2 minutes. Keep doing CPR and epinephrine. What else should the team do?
s.ok: Hunt for reversible causes: the Hs (hypoxia, hypovolaemia, hydrogen ions/acidosis, hypo/hyperkalaemia, hypothermia) and Ts (tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, thrombosis in heart or lungs). Fixing the cause is often the only way back.

fb.wait: In arrest, every second counts. Keep CPR going and look for causes.

sc.sub: PEA with a cause to find

s.msg: A 45-year-old who missed 2 dialysis sessions feels weak. Her ECG looks like this. Then she becomes unresponsive.
s.ok: Someone goes unresponsive: check breathing and pulse (no more than 10 seconds) while calling for help.

fb.cpr: Close, but confirm there's no pulse first (under 10 s).
fb.sugar: Not first. Check for a pulse.

s.msg: The monitor shows an organised rhythm, but there's NO pulse.
s.ok: Organised electrical activity without a pulse = PEA (pulseless electrical activity). Non-shockable: CPR + epinephrine ASAP.

fb.shock: PEA is not shockable. The electricity is already organised; the heart just isn't pumping.
fb.sync: She has no pulse. This is an arrest: CPR.

s.msg: CPR and epinephrine running. Before the arrest her ECG showed peaked T waves, and she missed dialysis. Most likely cause and fix?
s.ok: Hyperkalaemia (high potassium) is one of the Hs. Calcium stabilises the heart cell membranes within minutes, then insulin + glucose and other treatments push potassium into cells, and dialysis removes it.

fb.needle: That's for a tension pneumothorax (a T). No clues point there.
fb.ade: Adenosine is for SVT with a pulse.

s.msg: After treatment: pulse is back, BP 100/65.
s.ok: ROSC. Post-arrest care plus urgent dialysis to fix the cause.

fb.wait: She needs post-arrest care and dialysis now.

s.msg: A 70-year-old feels faint. Heart rate 34, BP 78/40, confused. He has a pulse.
s.ok: Slow rhythm WITH a pulse and signs of poor perfusion (low BP, confusion) = unstable bradycardia. First drug: atropine (blocks the vagus nerve's brake on the heart).

fb.shock: Never shock a patient with a pulse and a slow rhythm.
fb.cpr: He has a pulse. CPR is for no pulse (or rate too low to perfuse in kids).
fb.ade: Adenosine slows the heart even more. Dangerous here.

s.msg: Atropine didn't change anything. Still rate 34, BP 75/40.
s.ok: Complete heart block often doesn't respond to atropine (the block is below the AV node). Next: transcutaneous pacing (pads deliver small regular shocks to make the heart beat), or an epinephrine/dopamine infusion, then a transvenous or permanent pacemaker.

fb.atro: More atropine rarely helps in complete heart block. Move on to pacing.

s.msg: A 16-year-old's heart suddenly started racing in class. Rate 200, BP 118/76, she's talking and comfortable.
s.ok: Stable narrow-complex tachycardia. First try vagal manoeuvres: a strong strain (blowing into a syringe, then legs raised) boosts vagal tone and can break the AV node re-entry circuit.

fb.shock: She has a pulse and is stable. No shocks.
fb.epi: Epinephrine would make her heart faster.

s.msg: Vagal manoeuvre didn't work. Still 200, still stable.
s.ok: Adenosine: given as a fast IV push, it blocks the AV node for a few seconds (she'll feel a scary pause), which breaks the re-entry circuit. Works in most AVNRT.

s.msg: Different patient: same rhythm, but BP 70/40, chest pain, confused.
s.ok: Unstable tachycardia (low BP, chest pain, confusion) = synchronised cardioversion right away (with sedation if time). The shock is timed to the QRS so it doesn't land on the T wave and trigger VF.

fb.vagal: Too slow for an unstable patient.
